archetype.name: Pretender (record ahead of its play)
archetype.definition: Seattle holds a playoff spot in the Pacific on a 9-6-1 record, but it is being badly outshot and out-chanced at 5-on-5 and has stayed afloat on hot shooting and a few one-goal wins.

report.headline: A winning record on borrowed shooting; the possession numbers say trouble ahead
report.take:
Seattle sits third in the Pacific at 9-6-1, on pace for 97 points. That looks like a team that has turned a corner after finishing 31st on the site last year. The site doesn't buy it: the Kraken are 26th of 32 on the Teams tab. The record's foundation is thin. Their 57 goals scored exactly match their 57 allowed, so the goal differential is flat, and the underlying play is worse than flat. Seattle owns 43% of 5-on-5 shot attempts, dead last in the league, and 45% of expected goals, 27th.

What has kept the record above water is finishing. The skaters are shooting 13.0% in all situations, sixth in the league and well above the 11.6% league mark. The 5-on-5 PDO of 103.2 is the kind of number that tends to come back down. Pair that with 25.6 shots a game against 30.1 allowed and you have an offense converting a small volume at an unsustainable rate, in front of a defense that leaks. Add a +1.2 in Pts vs Goal Diff, with three of the last ten wins coming in overtime, and the record is running ahead of the goal margin, which is already running ahead of the play.

None of this is new. Last season's xGF % was 0.46 and its CF % 0.45, and the penalty kill was already poor at 72.2%. This year the kill has collapsed further to 65.1%, 30th, and neither goalie has bailed it out: Goalies GSAx is -1.9, with Joey Daccord at -2.6. The most encouraging individual signs are Berkly Catton, the only regular forward above 50% in expected-goal share at 0.566 and the team's best Game Score, and Brandon Montour, 28th of 252 defensemen on the site, playing over 24 minutes a night.

The slide may already be underway. Over the last five games Seattle went 2-3-0 and was outscored 20-13, and the scoring has dried up from October's 3.71 goals a game. A team that can't drive play depends on the shooting staying hot, and the shooting is the part of its game least likely to hold.

strengths.title: Finishing well above league rates
strengths.body: Seattle ranks ninth in goals per game despite ranking 26th in shots on goal, because its skaters are converting at 13.0%, sixth in the league. Depth is spread around: Freddy Gaudreau has 7 goals and Mackie Samoskevich 6. Little of this is structural, though. A team generating this few shots usually sees its shooting percentage drift back toward the league average.

strengths.title: A league-average power play
strengths.body: The power play is converting at 22.6%, 13th and essentially even with the league's 22.5%. That is a real step up from the sub-20% units of the past three seasons. Jordan Eberle (7 PP points) and Chandler Stephenson (6) are carrying it. It is the one special-teams unit that should hold roughly where it is.

strengths.title: Catton and Montour drive results
strengths.body: Berkly Catton leads the forwards with 14 points and a 12.5 Game Score, and his 0.566 xGF % stands alone on a roster where most regulars sit in the low 40s. Montour, 28th among the league's defensemen on the site, leads the blueline at 24.22 minutes a night. Both look like genuine contributors rather than shooting-luck stories.

concerns.title: Losing the puck and the chances
concerns.body: The 43% shot-attempt share is last in the league and the 45% expected-goal share is 27th. Seattle gives up 30.1 shots a game, 29th. This continues the last two seasons, when both shares were in the mid-40s, so it reads as the team's true level rather than a slow start. Records built on top of numbers like these tend to sink.

concerns.title: A penalty kill in freefall
concerns.body: Killing 65.1% of penalties ranks 30th, almost 12 points under the league's 77%. Last year's 72.2% was already weak, and it has gotten worse. Goaltending that is below expected on the shots it faces offers no cover, which helps explain why Seattle ranks 28th in goals allowed per game.

concerns.title: Goaltending and a center-heavy leak
concerns.body: Both goalies are under water on GSAx, Daccord at -2.6 with an .881 save %, Philipp Grubauer at -0.6. In front of them, the defense allows more points to centers than any team in the league, and its forwards overall rank 30th. Grubauer, 33rd on the goalies tab, looks like the better bet for more of the starts.

trend.note: An 8-6 October averaged 3.71 goals for and against, but the last five games have produced a 2-3-0 record and a -7 differential. The points % over that stretch is 0.194 below the season rate as the scoring cooled.

weekAhead.headline: Home-and-home with the league's best possession team
weekAhead.body:
The whole week is two games against Carolina: at home on the 12th, then in Raleigh on the 14th. The Hurricanes are 14-3-2, first on the site, and first in both 5-on-5 shares, owning 59% of shot attempts and 59.8% of expected goals. They lead the league with 33.3 shots a game and allow 22.4, second-fewest. That is the exact opposite of Seattle's profile. Their Pts vs Goal Diff of -0.6 says the record undersells them, if anything.

The Kraken's path is narrow. They need to convert their limited looks at the rate they have been, survive a heavy shot count against, and stay out of the box, because a 65.1% kill is a liability against anyone. Carolina's defense gives little to wingers and defensemen. Its weak spot, relatively, is centers, who take a larger share of the points against it than the league norm, which puts the onus on Catton, Beniers and Stephenson. Taking one of the two would be a good week. Getting swept is the most likely single outcome.

keyMatchups.title: Shot volume against Seattle's net
keyMatchups.body: Carolina leads the league in shots per game, and Seattle is 29th in shots allowed. The goalies have been below expected all year, so whoever starts will likely need his best game of the season. This is the matchup that most exposes the Kraken's structural problem.

keyMatchups.title: Seattle centers against Carolina's defense
keyMatchups.body: Carolina holds wingers and defensemen well under their usual output, ranking 4th and 2nd. Centers take 44.9% of the points against it, compared with 36.6% across the league. Catton, with the best expected-goal share on the roster, is the best candidate to exploit that.

keyMatchups.title: Special teams discipline
keyMatchups.body: Carolina's power play is middle of the pack at 22.2%. Against a Seattle kill at 65.1%, even an average unit becomes dangerous. Seattle's own power play, at 22.6%, faces an 85% Carolina kill, so the special-teams battle tilts toward the visitors' bench either way.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Seattle can keep the shot count against near its season average. If Carolina gets to the high 30s, the shooting luck won't be enough.

restOfSeason.body:
The 97-point pace is the most optimistic reading of this team. It rests on a PDO of 103.2 and a shooting percentage that ranks sixth, carried by a roster that ranks last in shot share and 27th in expected-goal share. As the finishing drifts toward the league rate, goals for should fall off while goals against stay high, and Seattle should play below .500 hockey in points over the remaining 66 games. I expect a finish in the 78-88 point range with 34-40 wins, and a goal differential per game that settles slightly negative, between -0.45 and -0.1.

What would change that is the penalty kill and the crease. A 65% kill is so far below the league that it is likely to improve somewhat on its own. A stretch of above-expected goaltending from Grubauer could keep the Kraken in the wild-card conversation in a Pacific with weak teams at the bottom. What won't change quickly is the possession deficit, which has now followed this team for three seasons.
swingFactors: How far the 13% shooting falls back toward league average
Whether the penalty kill recovers from 65%
Grubauer or Daccord delivering above-expected goaltending

confidence.note: Only 16 games played, but the possession deficit matches the last two seasons.
